name: Illusion of learning
statement: Study that feels easy is judged to be study that works, so learners rate fluent teaching and rereading above the harder methods that leave them remembering more.
meaning: Two claims sit inside the name. The first is that judgments of learning are built from how the material feels while it is being taken in. Smooth delivery, a second reading and a run of correct answers all raise the sense of knowing, and none of them is a measure of what will survive a week. The second is that the conditions producing durable learning tend to lower that feeling. Bjork and Bjork call those conditions desirable difficulties and list four: varying the conditions of practice, interleaving topics rather than blocking them, spacing rather than massing, and testing rather than presenting. Put the two claims together and the error is systematic rather than random. A learner sampling their own experience will rank the methods in roughly the reverse of the order that a delayed test would give. The word desirable carries weight. A difficulty the learner cannot meet stops helping, which is why this entry is about the calibration of the judgment and not about difficulty as a virtue.

origin.who: Arthur M. Glenberg, Alex Cherry Wilkinson and William Epstein
origin.note: Their paper is "The illusion of knowing: Failure in the self-assessment of comprehension", volume 10, issue 6, pages 597 to 602. Its full text could not be obtained for this entry and the citation was verified at Crossref, so nothing is said here about what it found. The study-strategy version of the idea is younger and belongs to Robert Bjork, who dates the term desirable difficulties to a chapter of his in 1994.

evidence: Bjork and Bjork set out the mechanism in a 2011 chapter. Rereading a chapter supplies familiarity and perceptual fluency, which the reader takes for comprehension, and conditions that make performance climb fast during practice are often the ones that fail at a delay. They cite Simon and Bjork's keystroke study, where learners given blocked practice were overconfident about the next day's test. Learners given interleaved practice predicted their own scores closely. They also cite Rohrer and Taylor on volume formulas, at 63% correct a week later after interleaved instruction against 20% after blocked. Both figures are quoted here from that chapter and not from the papers. Kornell and Bjork measured the gap directly. In Experiment 1a, 120 UCLA undergraduates saw 72 paintings, six by each of 12 artists, for 3 seconds apiece, with half the artists massed and half interleaved, then identified the painter of new works. On the first test block, spaced study gave .61 correct against .35, t(119) = 10.82, d = 0.99, and Experiment 1b reproduced it between subjects with 72 participants at .59 against .36, t(70) = 4.94, d = 1.28. Then the questionnaire. Of the 120, 78% had done better in the spaced condition and 78% said massing had been as good as spacing or better. A style-recognition version with 80 participants gave hits of .77 against .67, t(79) = 3.28, d = 0.41, and of the 72 who expressed a preference, 64 picked massing. Asked afterwards which artists had been massed, 28 participants scored .74 for spaced artists and .55 for massed ones, t(27) = 1.19, p = .25. The judgment was not a memory of the schedule. It was a reading of how study had felt. Carpenter, Wilford, Kornell and Mullaney moved the cue to the teacher. Forty-two Iowa State undergraduates watched one of two 65-second videos of the same speaker explaining why calico cats are female, upright and without notes or hunched over a podium reading haltingly. Predicted recall was higher after the fluent version, t(40) = 3.34, p = .002, d = 1.03. Actual recall of the 10 idea units did not differ, t < 0.50. Overconfidence ran at .22 against .03, t(40) = 3.02, p = .004, d = 0.93. In a second experiment with 70 students, test scores were .44 against .40, t(68) = 0.81, p = .42, and time spent studying the script afterwards was 1.39 minutes against 1.43. Deslauriers, McCarty, Miller, Callaghan and Kestin ran the classroom version. In two semesters of calculus-based introductory physics at Harvard, 149 of 157 students were randomly split for two 90-minute meetings in week 12, one on static equilibrium and one on fluids. Both rooms got identical slides, handouts and worked solutions from instructors trained in both styles; the only variable was whether students attempted the problems in small groups first or were told how to solve them. Each class ended with a feeling-of-learning survey and a 12-question test written by an author who had not seen the materials. Students in the active rooms scored 0.46 standard deviations higher on the test and reported 0.56 standard deviations lower feeling of learning, both P < 0.001. The models controlled for prior physics knowledge, attitudes, two earlier midterms and gender. Adding perceived teaching effectiveness to the model absorbed the effect: that rating predicted feeling of learning at 0.51, P < 0.001, and active against passive stopped predicting it. Seventeen students interviewed afterwards described the active classes as disjointed and lacking flow, 15 of 17, and all but one found the passive lecture easier to follow.

replication.headline: The strategy version reproduces. The classroom version has gone both ways: Boedeker's crossover trial with 146 medical students found feeling of learning 0.56 standard deviations higher in the active session, the same size as Deslauriers's gap and the opposite sign.
replication.detail: Boedeker and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine copied the design and credit Deslauriers for it. Second-year medical students, 146 of them, were randomised across two days of 50-minute sessions, hypertension on one day and electrocardiogram interpretation on the other. Each student took one session as a lecture and one as a large-group interactive class, on the same clinical vignettes and the same slides. Each session ended with a feeling-of-learning survey and a 12-question test built by faculty who had not seen the lesson materials. Learners scored 0.27 standard deviations higher after the interactive session, 95% CI [0.07, 0.47], p = 0.010. Their feeling of learning was 0.56 standard deviations higher, p < 0.001, with all four survey items pointing the same way on both days. The authors attribute the reversal to the stage of learner, since their participants held degrees and a year of medical school. The instructor-fluency leg is unsettled inside the laboratory that found it. Carpenter, Mickes, Rahman and Fernandez repeated the manipulation with a 22-minute lecture and tested at three delays. The fluent instructor was rated higher on organisation, knowledge, preparedness and effectiveness in all three experiments, with d from .53 to 1.26. Judgments of learning did not follow: 62% against 62%, t(68) = .05, then 44% against 48%, t(100) = .99, p = .33, then 63% against 57%, t(89) = 1.55, p = .12. Test scores were 66% against 65%, then 56% against 62%, then 60% against 52%, t(89) = 2.07, p = .041, d = .43. Carpenter, Northern, Tauber and Toftness later reported two more experiments in which lecture fluency did inflate judgments of learning without moving test scores. Instructor experience made no difference. That result is taken here from the abstract at Europe PMC rather than the paper.

study.cite: Boedeker, P., Schlingmann, T., Kailin, J., Nair, A., Foldes, C., Rowley, D., Salciccioli, K., Maag, R., Moreno, N., & Ismail, N. (2024). Active versus passive learning in large-group sessions in medical school: A randomized cross-over trial investigating effects on learning and the feeling of learning. Medical Science Educator, 35(1), 459-467.

limits: The two classroom studies do not measure the same thing, and the coincidence of 0.56 hides it. Deslauriers's composite came from four items about perceived learning. Boedeker's adapted composite keeps one of them and adds enjoyment of the session, a rating of the instructor and a wish that all courses were taught that way. A student who liked the class registers there as a student who felt they learned. Both tests were multiple choice and taken in the room minutes after the teaching, so neither speaks to retention. Deslauriers's design also moved both groups away from their normal class, which usually mixed lecturing with occasional activities, and the passive lecture was built to maximise fluency of delivery. The intervention at the end of that paper is self-report from a later course, at 65% of students reporting improved feelings about active learning and 75% crediting the presentation, with no control group. Kornell and Bjork's participants were UCLA undergraduates sorting paintings by unfamiliar artists, and Carpenter's watched a 65-second video about cats; how far either travels to a syllabus is untested there. No multi-site or registered replication of any of these results was located. That search covered Crossref and OpenAlex by title and DOI, Europe PMC, and the web under "feeling of learning", "illusion of knowing", "instructor fluency" and "judgments of learning". Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell's 2013 Annual Review of Psychology survey, the standard reference for the area, is paywalled. Yan, Bjork and Bjork's 2016 paper on how hard these beliefs are to correct is closed at every location OpenAlex lists. Neither is quoted here.
misreadings: The finding is not that students dislike learning or that discomfort is the active ingredient. Bjork and Bjork's word is desirable, and a difficulty beyond what the learner can meet is on their account an undesirable one. This atlas records both halves of that. The testing-effect entry notes that retrieval which mostly fails buys nothing, and the disfluency-effect entry records that setting a problem in hard-to-read type failed to improve reasoning in 2,580 people. Difficulty is a by-product of the useful conditions, not the mechanism. A second error is to read the feeling as uninformative. In Carpenter's three-experiment follow-up the correlation between students' judgments and their test scores was positive every time, from r = .30 to r = .44. The judgment is biased by a cue, which is a different claim from the judgment being noise. A third is to treat this as the Dunning-Kruger effect in a classroom. Deslauriers reports that students with more prior physics knowledge showed a stronger positive link between feeling and performance, which is adjacent. The driver measured in these studies is the fluency of the material and its delivery, not the learner's skill. The fourth is the one that gets quoted from the Harvard paper. Its 0.46 standard deviations is a within-class result on a 12-item quiz taken at the end of a single 90-minute meeting, not a course grade and not a delayed measure. The broader claim that active learning outperforms lecturing rests on Freeman and colleagues' meta-analysis of 225 studies. It put examination and concept-inventory performance 0.47 standard deviations higher across 158 studies, and the odds of failing at 1.95 under traditional lecturing across 67. That is the evidence for the learning half. Deslauriers's contribution is the feeling half.
